summary:
Tucumán stands under Argentina's national framework, and no Tucumán-specific rule material enough to depart from it is sourced here. Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012, permits a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, so an adult visitor's identity documents are not gated by medical sign-off.

That statutory position has been narrowed by executive action. A decree issued on 5 February 2025 restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone treatment, and a second decree governs the housing of transgender people in prisons. Legal experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the minors' measure illegal and unconstitutional and signalled an intention to seek judicial intervention; the litigation outcome is not sourced here.

Violence risk is the sharper practical concern. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio LGBT+ recorded at least 227 bias-motivated crimes against LGBT people in 2025, a record and an increase on 2024, averaging one every 38 hours. Trans women and travestis accounted for 62.5% of victims (142 people), trans men for 18 cases against 5 in 2024, with 13 lesbians and 4 non-binary people also targeted. Physical violence made up 64.8% of cases (147), and 32% occurred inside police stations or penal institutions. Police involvement rose from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025.

Trans activists interviewed on 4 April 2025 described a chaotic and desperate situation, with heightened exposure to violence, discrimination and poverty under the Milei government's policies.

The judicial response to gender-motivated killing is contested. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance removed by an appeals court in 2020, so that aggravation is not currently applied in that line of cases.
tangentialFactors:
President Milei eliminated the federal Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry and dismissed trans employees hired under the Trans Labour Quota Law, which had reserved at least 1% of public-sector jobs for trans people. The removal of that institutional channel sits alongside the 2025 decrees as the background against which activists describe the current situation.

Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records negative assessments for same-sex relations, gender recognition and the registration of civil-sexuality organisations, with an assessment of deterioration against the earlier statutory position. The United Nations described Law 26.743 as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region when it passed, and Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010.

Anti-discrimination protection exists through a combination of national and provincial laws, though the sources do not set out how Tucumán's own anti-discrimination provisions are applied in practice.
localsOnly:
Residents of Tucumán face the same 5 February 2025 decree restricting gender-affirming surgery and hormone treatment for adolescents as the rest of Argentina, and the second decree governing where transgender people are held in prisons. Both were issued by the national executive rather than by the Tucumán authorities.

The Trans Labour Quota Law's reservation of at least 1% of public-sector jobs for trans people has been undercut by the dismissal of trans employees and the elimination of the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry, which affects resident employment and access to a dedicated federal interlocutor.

Legal gender recognition for adults remains available under Law 26.743 without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, and that pathway is unchanged for residents of the province.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Tucumán-specific source is present in the inventory: there is no reporting on provincial police conduct, provincial hate-crime prosecutions, or the availability of gender-marker changes through the Tucumán registry. The province is treated as carrying the national position, which is an absence of sourced deviation rather than a sourced finding of identical practice.

The 227-case 2025 total is a national figure from the Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio LGBT+; the inventory does not break it down by province, so Tucumán's share of those cases is unresolved.

Whether the constitutional challenge to the February 2025 minors' decree has been decided is unresolved on these sources, as is the current status of the travesticidio aggravating circumstance beyond the April 2025 Supreme Court ruling in the Sacayán case.

Provincial anti-discrimination law in Tucumán is referenced only in general terms as part of a national-plus-provincial combination; its text, penalties and enforcement record are not sourced.
